statement: Any set of at most $n-1$ shares is uniformly distributed on $(\{0,1\}^\ell)^{n-1}$
For every $0\le k<n$, any set of $k$ shares is uniformly distributed on $(\{0,1\}^\ell)^k$
idea: Missing share $s_j$ is itself $s\oplus(\text{XOR of the others})$. Whatever the other shares are, $s_j$ is a one-time-pad encryption of $s$ under the uniform key $\bigoplus_{i\neq j}s_i$; by 2.3 its distribution is the same for every secret, and the other $n-2$ shares are uniform and independent of everything. So any $n-1$ shares have the same law for every $s$.

Correctness follows by XORing all $n$ shares: every sampled share cancels twice, leaving $s$. Privacy concerns the joint law of the observed tuple, not independence of the determined final share from all other shares. The constant-preimage argument below proves the joint law is uniform and independent of the secret, and then covers smaller observed subsets by marginalization.
